title: Time-critical small parts: the eye and the scrotum
summary: Two presentations where minutes matter and the bedside scan helps, if you know its limits: sudden visual symptoms and the acute scrotum. Learn the safe technique, the dynamic signs, and why neither scan should delay the specialist.
author: Dr Firas Abou-Auda, Consultant in Emergency Medicine and Course Director, Wavelength
conflicts: Dr Firas Abou-Auda is Course Director of Wavelength, which runs paid ultrasound courses.
audience: Emergency, acute and urgent care doctors, advanced clinical practitioners and physician associates who assess eye and scrotal emergencies.
outcomes: Scan the eye safely, within ophthalmic output limits and with no pressure on the globe
Separate retinal detachment, posterior vitreous detachment and vitreous haemorrhage using after-movements
Scan the scrotum and spermatic cord in a systematic, side-to-side way
Recognise the signs of testicular torsion and epididymo-orchitis, and the limits of colour Doppler
Escalate without delay, whatever the scan shows, when the clinical picture demands it
references: Lahham S, et al. Point-of-care ultrasonography in the diagnosis of retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, and vitreous detachment in the emergency department. JAMA Network Open. 2019;2:e192162.
